findings.title: The `unset` remediation contradicts the delete rule and removes the developer's value
findings.description:
The design says delete "mirrors write — deletes from whichever project file the key's scope maps to" (line 89). For `git.integration_branch` that file is `.context-forge.local.toml`. Two later parts of the doc rely on the opposite behaviour:
- The collision rule (line 146) tells the user that clearing the stale shared copy "is a separate, explicit `cf config unset <key> --project`".
- Walkthrough step 9 (line 259) runs `cf config unset git.integration_branch --project` "to clear the stale shared-file copy explicitly, then confirm `cf check` is clean".

Under the routing as written, that command deletes the personal value (`legacy/value`) and leaves the stale shared value in place. The read fallback (lines 79, 140) then resolves the stale `another-legacy-value`. So the developer's preference is lost and the old value comes back without any warning, which is the harm the collision rule exists to prevent. The `cf check` warning also stays. The same gap affects any project that has not migrated yet: a personal key that lives only in the shared file cannot be unset at all.

To fix this, choose one rule and state it:
- (a) Delete of a personal key also removes it from the shared file, so delete clears every project-level copy. This matches what a user means by "unset" and keeps the walkthrough as it is.
- (b) Have `migrate-personal` itself delete the stale shared copy in the collision case, since the personal value already wins at read time, and remove the `unset` advice.

Option (b) is lighter and also removes the separate "skipped" reporting path. After choosing, update line 146 and walkthrough step 9 to match.

findings.title: Projects that already exist never get the gitignore line, so the personal file can still be committed
findings.description:
The slice says it will "keep personal settings out of git" (line 19). The only thing that adds the ignore line is `cf init` (lines 32, 157–159). The projects this slice is for are already initialized and have the key committed. When one of their developers runs `cf config set git.integration_branch … --project` or `cf config migrate-personal`, a new `.context-forge.local.toml` is created that nothing ignores, and the next `git add -A` commits it.

The cheapest fix inside the current scope is to reuse the one-line gitignore helper. Either call it from `migrate-personal` and from the first write to the personal file in `ConfigManager.set`, or extend the new `ConsistencyChecker` rule to warn when `.context-forge.local.toml` exists but is not ignored. That still adds only the one line, so it does not overlap the broader gitignore item listed under Future Work.

findings.title: Data Flow read step 2 is written as a condition that is always true
findings.description: Step 2 checks the shared file "only if the key's own scope is `shared`, OR it's a personal key falling through from step 1 with no value yet found there." Taken together with step 1, that covers every key. In practice the rule is simply: personal file (personal keys only), then shared file, then user, then default. The "only if … OR …" wording suggests a filter that is not there, and an implementer may add a check that skips the shared file for personal keys. That would break the pre-migration fallback that Migration Plan item (a) depends on. Restate the step as the plain sequence.

findings.title: The `scope` field name is also used for a different concept
findings.description: `ConfigKeyDefinition.scope: 'shared' | 'personal'` sits next to the existing `ConfigManager.set/delete(key, value, scope: 'user' | 'project')` parameter (`ConfigManager.ts:165`, `:187`). Inside `ConfigManager` the routing code will compare both in the same function. A distinct name such as `visibility` or `sharing` would avoid the clash and follows the project's semantic-naming rule. This does not block anything.

findings.title: The dependency differs from the slice plan entry
findings.description: The frontmatter declares `dependencies: [914]`, but the 915 entry in the slice plan says "Dependencies: none". 914 is complete and the slice's reason for depending on it is sound (line 45). Consider updating the plan entry so the two documents agree.
